utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Are there any preliminaries? I did understand that the Prosecution would like to make a submission on P7331, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. Mr. Traldi, to whom you addressed the inquiry, will address the Court, and I'm going to ask him to move over here where I think it will be easier to communicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. And thank you for giving me the time to address the matter which the President raised at the end of Thursday's session. Our position is that the portions of Witness Boric's OTP interview that we eventually tender are admissible for all purposes and should be admitted for all purposes by the Trial Chamber under Rule 89(C) rather than Rule 92 ter, bis, or quater consistent with what we understand to have been the practice in this trial. The Tribunal's jurisprudence holds prior inconsistent statements admissible for the truth of their contents and holds that Rules 92 bis, ter and quater do not apply in these circumstances. I'd point to, for instance, the following authorities: Paragraph 31 of the Popovic Appeals Chamber decision of the 1st of February, 2008; the Limaj trial decision of 25 April 2005; the Seselj trial decision of 11 September 2008; guidance in the Gotovina case issued on the 30th of March, 2010; paragraph 19 of the Gotovina Trial Judgement; and paragraph 1289 of the Djordjevic Trial Judgement. And if it would assist, I'm prepared to discuss the implications of a couple of those decisions briefly if it would be useful to the Chamber and to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If could you do that briefly, you're invited to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Popovic and Limaj decisions, which were both made in the context of a party's cross-examination of adverse witnesses that it had called to the stand itself, addressed the issue in some detail. Those decisions rejected requests to apply what they described as a traditional common law rule against the admissibility of prior inconsistent statements for the truth of their contents, noting both that such a rule is, in those decisions' view, inapplicable to a mixed system where fact-finding is made by professional judges rather than by juries and noting the recent trend even in common law countries towards admitting prior inconsistent statements for all purposes. One example of the evaluation of such evidence can be found in the Djordjevic trial judgement regarding official notes conducted by a working group of RJB Serbia, and the Djordjevic Appeals Chamber in paragraphs 395 through 397 of the appeals judgement explicitly addressed the Trial Chamber's reliance on those notes, the Trial Chamber's analysis of those notes, and found the Trial Chamber did not err in rejecting contradictory witness evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you kindly slow down for the interruption. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise. And did not err in relying on those notes for a set of meetings for which they were the only evidence. Our understanding of the approach in this trial is based in part on the Chamber's guidance of 19 June 2012, which encouraged the parties if they were concerned about the possibility of witnesses recanting previously given evidence to lead the witnesses viva voce and then tender their previously given evidence as prior inconsistent statements consistent with the jurisprudence of the Tribunal; in other words, as we understood it, to tender such prior statements for the truth of their contents consistent with the Popovic and Limaj decisions, among others, that I'd referred to earlier. More recently, the Chamber inquired as to what purpose Miodrag Dragutinovic's previous statements, P7156 and P7157, were being tendered. The Prosecution took the position that the material should come in for all purposes. We understand the Chamber to have accepted that position. Turning briefly to the specific instance. Mr. Boric's evidence is a paradigmatic case for the admission of prior statements for all purposes. His prior statements were made in an audio recorded interview in which he was informed of his rights, asked if he wished to have a lawyer present, advised that if he chose to answer questions his answers would be recorded and could be used in evidence. These prior statements thus have substantial indicia of reliability. The Trial Chamber can evaluate his statements in light of his testimony both in general and on the same points and in light of other evidence in the record and determine the credibility of specific evidence provided during his interview and during his testimony on that basis. Now, just as a note, regarding that reliability point, we don't always tender, for instance, a witness's solemn declaration when we tender parts of previous testimony because we understand, and I think the Defence will confirm, that there is no dispute that testimony at ICTY is given pursuant a solemn declaration. In this instance to facilitate the Chamber's review, we would intend to tender portions of the interview which reflect the procedural safe-guards that I mentioned above. Just to discuss one example very briefly regarding the operation including the massacre in Biljani. Looking at his testimony, Mr. Boric first claimed he was not aware of the operation at all. Later, after saying he probably or maybe stood by portions of his interview related to the details of that operation, testified that he was probably aware of it as it was being carried out. The Chamber, of course, can evaluate all of that evidence together and determine what of his evidence it attaches weight to. For completeness, Your Honours, there is one instance I'm aware of where we've indicated that we would not rely on a prior inconsistent statement for the truth of its contents. I'd respectfully submit that instance supports this interpretation of the jurisprudence. We made that representation in the context of a prior statement by Witness Veselinovic, which we put to him, and he agreed, contained a number of untruthful statements, to the point that our case, as we put it to him, was that "almost nothing in the statement is true." Our representation was specific to that instance and would not have been necessary except that previous inconsistent statements otherwise are admissible for the truth of their contents. We were simply making clear on the record that there was no dispute that the contents of that statement, now P6910, were not true before asking the Chamber to rule on admission. And that had the effect of clarifying we were not in the typical situation where such statements are admitted for all purposes. We'd submit, however, that we are in that typical situation here, as we were with the other witnesses with whom this issue has arisen. Witness Boric's previous interview and the portions used with him during court are relevant, reliable, and admissible for the truth of their contents, in our submission, pursuant to Rule 89(C). And that completes the submission I'd intended to make on the matter, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Could I take you back to page 2, line 24, 25, and then the first lines of page 3. Could you repeat them because I think that not all of it is recorded. You started by saying: "One example of the evaluation of such evidence can be found ..." And could you resume from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can be found in the Djordjevic trial judgement. That Trial Chamber was analysing Official Notes taken by a working group of RJB Serbia. They were admitted for all purposes. And it analysed those notes and the weight to be afforded them in its judgement; for instance, in paragraphs 1289 and 2113. The Djordjevic Appeals Chamber in paragraphs 395 through 397 ... and this portion appears to be included in its entirety. So I can repeat it, but I'm not sure if it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think that's on the record, but there was a large missing part. That's now on the transcript. I would have -- in relation to that specific portion, I would have the following question. SJB notes are not taken for Tribunal purposes. Isn't it true that at least --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: RJB. That at least at some points in time the fact whether a statement was taken for Tribunal purposes or was taken by other agencies made a difference, and therefore I wonder to what extent when relying on these Official Notes whether that is similar to the situation we have here where the interview was conducted by Tribunal officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd referred to that -- and I take the point, Mr. President. Thank you for giving me the opportunity to respond. I'd referred to the Djordjevic example to illustrate how trial chambers have addressed such evidence regarding the admissibility of prior inconsistent statements taken for Tribunal purposes. The Seselj decision to which I referred earlier, for instance, addresses that question squarely. And I think the Gotovina guidance in citing the Seselj decision, at least implicitly, adopts that rationale. And I can check whether the other cases -- I don't remember at the moment the source of the statements at issue in Limaj, and in -- and in Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Stojanovic, any response.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a couple of sentences, Your Honours. Good morning. We carefully followed the arguments referring to the prosecutor's suggestions using -- in relation to the evidence in the cross-examination of Mr. Boric. We are taking into account the arguments and we would like to quote court practice. The fact is that at this point we have different standpoints on the application of Rule 89 of the Rules, so we would kindly ask you to give us until Monday so that we could state our position on this proposal by the Prosecution. I come from a different system in Bosnia and Herzegovina prompting me to take a different position, and I understand the Prosecution's position, so that is why we would like to have time, until Monday, to be able to state our own response to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have until Monday. I immediately add to that, Mr. Stojanovic, that the fact that you come from a different system not necessarily prompts you to take a different position because all parties are supposed to rely on the practice developed in this Tribunal. Please keep that in mind, but we'll hear from you by next Monday. Any other matter to be raised? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I don't know if my learned friend finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I -- I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My topic is not even close interesting legally as the previous one. I just wanted to draw your attention, Your Honours, that we were scheduled to sit on May 22nd as a way of compensation for the next non-working week. But since this next week is working for us now, we have to go into the field in regard of re-opening of the Tomasica case. We think that there is nothing to be compensated, and we would ask to -- for our organisational purposes, bringing witnesses, buying the tickets, going into the field, to ask you whether you would reconsider your decision to sit on Friday, 22nd of May this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, when we considered to compensate for other days, that was in an earlier stage. The Chamber has decided that we'll set on the 20 May as scheduled, although -- the 22nd of May. We'll sit as scheduled, although the context in which this decision is now to be considered is slightly different from when we gave that decision. Many other days we're not sitting which were not known yet when we decided to sit on the 22nd of May, so the compensation issue may have been slightly changed, but we'll sit on the 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No other preliminaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very briefly, and the witness, I assume, can be brought in for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness already be escorted into the courtroom. That would be Mr. Andric, I take it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Purely for the record a leftover matter from Witness Boric's testimony. At the end of the first session on Thursday, I'd used 65 ter 32447 which I neglected to tender. I am sure my friends may need a little bit of time to express a position, but I'd just ask that we be informed if there are any objections to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, are you already in a position to respond or would you rather take the next 48 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be a good thing to wait, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber would like to hear within the next 48 hours. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Andric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andric. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. The Court may have anticipated me, I don't know, but I think a 90(E) advisement would be appropriate in this instance as was the case in previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the protection of your own witness, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Andric, before we start hearing your evidence, I'd like to draw your attention to Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and I'll first read it to you. It reads: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." This means that if a question is put to you and if you would think that a truthful answer might tend to incriminate yourself, that you may address me and ask to be relieved from answering that question. The Chamber will then decide whether you are or not. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find Mr. Stojanovic standing to your left. And Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Andric.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since we both speak relatively quickly, I would like to ask you to try to be as slow as possible because of the transcript. And I would like to ask you, as is customary here, to tell us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: My name is Svetozar Andric, son of Petko.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, Mr. Andric, if at one point you told Mr. Karadzic's Defence -- or you provided a written statement to the Karadzic Defence and you answered questions which were put to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at 65 ter 1D04788 in e-court, please. And could we also look at the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, do you recognise the signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the date on the left-hand side of the document, what about that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: The 16th of July, 2013.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that something that you wrote in your own hand?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, did you have the opportunity to read the statement again while you were preparing to appear before the Tribunal today?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now that you have refreshed your recollection about the contents of the statement, if I were to put the same questions to you now as were put to you then and after having given the solemn declaration to speak the truth and nothing but the truth, would you give identical answers to those questions that were then put to you?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And would those answers be the full truth and your full knowledge about the matters that you spoke about in answer to the questions that were then put to you?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender the statement of Andric, Svetozar which bears the 65 ter number 1D04788.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement receives number D1033.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would also like to tender three accompanying documents which bears 65 ter numbers 04702, 1D04789, and 1D04790.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 04702 receives number D1034. 1D4789 receives number D1035. And 1D4790 receives number D1036.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1034 through D1036 are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. With your leave, I would like to read the summary of the statement of Svetozar Andric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Short summary, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within the guide-lines that you set. Witness Svetozar Andric is a professional military officer and is retired now in the rank of lieutenant-general. He joined the VRS on the 19th of May, 1992 -- actually, there, since 19th of May 1992, he performed during the war and after the war a series of responsible duties beginning as commander of the Birac Brigade, then he was the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, and then retired in 2002 from the post of commander of the VRS 5th Corps. In his statement, he will talk about the beginning of the war in the Birac area about the forming of the VRS units in that area after the JNA left, about the time and manner in which brigades were organised, brigades which later joined the Drina Corps. He will explain the documents dating from May and June 1992 which refer to questions and problems in the system of command and control and particularly those relating to unity of command in those initial days. He will explain his position during his testimony in the setting up of the camp for prisoners of war Susica, about the problems of the population that was moving out, and the treatment of prisoners of war. He will also talk about the intensity of the fighting with the enemy in the area of responsibility of his unit, and about crimes against the Serbian population in the Birac area. He will also talk about the tasks, the role, and the movements of his unit in the Krivaja 95 action. He will describe in detail the movements of his units as well as his personal participation in the action, starting from the 5th of July, 1995, in the broader sector of Srebrenica, the intelligence data about the strength of the enemy who did not abide by their obligation to demilitarise the enclave, about the meeting with General Mladic in the Viogor village sector, the order to continue the action towards Zepa, and the fighting that his unit waged in this sector. He returned to the headquarters in Sekovici with his unit on the 2nd of August, 1995. And on the 6th of August, 1995, the hand-over of duty of the brigade commander took place between him and the new commander, after which he practically took over the post of Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps to which he was appointed in the interim by an establishment decree. Now, I would like to put some questions to the witness in order to clarify a couple of things from the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us please focus on paragraph 13, D1033.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I cannot see it on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You'll see it very quickly, General. Paragraph 13 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could you please zoom in a bit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see it now, General?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but I'd need to have bigger letters, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph, you speak about the situation in the eastern part of Birac and the central area at Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Glogova. In order to make your statement as concrete as possible, please tell us about the torched Serb villages and the number of victims. Where did you get these figures when you gave such an answer in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, esteemed Mr. Stojanovic, in view of the time that we have available, it's probably limited, I will try to refer to a particular period when the Serb people suffered, that is the period from end of September 1992 until mid-January 1993. In order for this to be clearer to you, we shall start from the 24th of September, 1991, when a purely Serb village, Podravanje, in the municipality of Vlasenica, was torched. On that occasion, 70 Serb houses were torched, 32 persons lost their lives, 16 were wounded, 43 went missing, 94 managed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, I stop you. The question was where did you get the figures? You are now explaining what happened, but the question was a different one. Could you tell us where did you get those figures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour, I will say that. But in order to have a full answer, I need to provide an explanation. This information comes from the documentation centre Republika Srpska, so I kindly ask -- I'll be very brief, but in the coming period it's very important for me to explain all of this. Then on the 26th in the municipality of Vlasenica, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, what is important for us is what is asked, and you've answered that question, that you got the figures from this documentation centre. And if Mr. Stojanovic wants to know further details, he'll ask you. Mr. Stojanovic, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask General Andric to focus on page 15, line 23 of today's transcript. What happened in the village of Podravanje that you spoke about? Did that happen on the 24th of September 1991 or in 1992.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: It happened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to clarify the record while we are still here. General, sir, in view of the time and the way in which we function in this courtroom, my next question will be as follows. The data that you have and that you tried to analyse according to events, village, et cetera, is that what you speak of in paragraph 13, the number of killed civilians and the number of Serb villages torched?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just wish to speak about this concrete period; that is to say, from September 1992 until January 1993. I would like to continue along those lines. After the 24th came the 26th and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, no. It's not for you to decide what is relevant and important at this moment. That's for the parties. So unless specifically asked about a certain event, you should just answer the questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is going to be my next question precisely, but please bear in mind what you have just been told. Give us specifically these events that you wish to refer to and that add up to this number.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: The 26th in Vlasenica, the attack on Rogosija, 29 people were killed and 30 were wounded and an entire Serb village was torched and property destroyed. Then on the 6th of November an attack from Kamenica. The attack was carried out by Naser Oric personally with his troops from Srebrenica, 120 persons were killed, most of them civilians, five villages were torched. Pathologists from the military medical academy documented that. That is a crime that is unheard of. Then on the 14th of December, the attack against the municipality of Bratunac where Sikiric, Loznica, and Bjelovac were torched - three villages, therefore - 58 persons were killed, 70 were wounded. All of these three villages were looted and torched. Then the attack against the local commune of Kravica on the 7th of January, 1992; that is to say -- actually, 1993. Sorry. On Orthodox Christmas Day. 48 persons were killed and over 50 were wounded and four were taken prisoner. 17 Serb villages were torched and looted. Then the municipality of Skelani was destroyed -- or rather attacked. The local commune, rather, of Skelani. Then 62 persons were killed, 82 persons were wounded, 5 were taken to a camp for civilians, and over there in prison in Srebrenica two were killed on the spot due to the beatings they had suffered. The total number of victims is 371, fatalities that is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the number, how many Serb villages were torched.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is only within five months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. The interpreters did not catch how much villages were torched. Could you give the numbers again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 33 with regard to these six events.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I would just like to say one more thing. In the municipalities of Skelani and Bratunac, up until 1993, the month of March, about 1322 persons were killed. Out of them, 750 were civilians; 522 were military conscripts. If we look at the percentage, we will see that 12 per cent of the fatalities were women. Also 12 per cent were over 65. And 3 per cent were children that were under age. So the question is: Could these people have been armed? Could they have taken part in armed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- first of all, Mr. Tieger, is there dispute about -- that in a large number of villages in that period of time a large number of Muslims, Muslim civilians were killed -- Serbs. I'm ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Without respect to particular statistics, I think the Court is well aware of the fact that the -- and I believe that question was answered most recently I think by Mr. Traldi in a similar -- or maybe Mr. Jeremy in a similar situation posed by the Court. Of course, there's no dispute that there were atrocities on both sides or all sides to the conflict at various times and during this period of time as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would not cross-examine the witness in order to test the reliability of those figures?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's not my intention, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, this also demonstrates - and for you, Witness, as well - it demonstrates that it's a waste of time what we are doing now because there's no dispute about larger numbers of Serb civilians being killed in a large number of villages during that period of time. Mr. Stojanovic, you -- you could have known this. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't hear today from my learned friend from the Prosecution that this is not in dispute, the number of victims, the places --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the question is whether all the specific locations, whether those are relevant or not, the way in which it is presented, I think, finds no -- no dispute with the Prosecution apart, perhaps, from details, and I thought that that's the gist of what this witness wanted to tell us as we find it in his statement. I think I was clear that we don't have to know the names of one -- all 150 Serb villages, neither would it assist us to have a calculation which amounts exactly to thousands. That you didn't hear it today from the -- earlier from the Prosecution is most likely because you didn't ask, and the parties are invited and are expected to focus on what really is in dispute. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us please take a look at paragraph 17 of the witness's statement, that is now D1033. Paragraph 17. Just a brief question for the sake of clarification, Mr. Andric.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say around the middle of paragraph 17: "On the 8th of July, the unit was ordered to carry out the task along the axis of Jasenovac-Caurka-Kostur-Alibegovac." I would like to ask you to tell the Trial Chamber whether this axis along your unit moved, as you were ordered in the task issued on the 8th of July, did that include the villages that were inside or outside the boundaries of the enclave according to the demilitarisation agreement from 1993?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Specifically these villages, Klokoc, Caurka, Kostur, were outside the protected area. These were fortifications of the enemy. We had fighting there and that was precisely one of the objectives, to separate the two enclaves, to resolve the issue of these three locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd like to finish by asking you something about paragraph 26 of your statement. Please take a look at paragraph 26 of your statement. That is to say, D1033. Mr. Andric, you speak about the hand-over of duty here and also where you went after that. However, I would like to ask you for the sake of clarification to tell us in a bit more detail what your duties were and where you went from the 8th of August, 1995, onwards; that is to say, when you were appointed Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Stojanovic, after receiving duty on the 8th of August, in the period from the 14th and 15th of August, I was in Krajina. At that time, there was one unit from the Drina Corps that was helping out there. My wife's brother was killed there on that occasion. I was supposed to get him out, but I didn't manage to. Then on the 16th of September until the 22nd, I was in the area of Novi Grad, Bosanski Novi in order to pull out 60 of our soldiers who had remained encircled there. After arriving in the command of the Drina Corps on the 26th of September and then until the 20th of October, I was in the area of the Krajina, Mrkonjic Grad, Kljuc with a tactical unit, a tactical group, at brigade level, where I was in charge on behalf of the Drina Corps to lead that group. On the 20th of October, I returned to the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andric. And those would be the questions the Defence had for you at this point in time. Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Andric, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Tieger. You find Mr. Tieger to your right. Mr. Tieger is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, General. We have about ten minutes before our first recess --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- so I'll address a few questions until that point. In addition to your previous testimony in the Karadzic case, which Mr. Stojanovic mentioned, you also testified about some of the events described in your statement in this Court before -- in Belgrade in the trial of Mr. Grujic and Branko Popovic, among others - that is, Branko Popovic also known as Marko Pavlovic - in January 2007; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you testified under oath in that proceeding; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And so I presume your position is that you also told the truth to that court?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the time we have, I wanted to ask you about some of the backdrop to a number of the orders that are mentioned; that is, the orders in late May by you that are mentioned in your statement. So first of all, this Court has received evidence, that's P2799, that on the 12th of May, 1992, the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina made a decision on forming the Army of the Serbian Republic, and Article 2 of that decision provided that former units and staffs of Territorial Defence are renamed into commands and units of the army whose organisation and formation will be established by the president of the republic. That's consistent with your understanding of what transpired at that time.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the 18th of May in a meeting with General Mladic which is reflected in his notebook, he told you that you were going to be the commander of the Birac Brigade; correct? And that's P352, e-court pages 356 through 358 in English and 366 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you, indeed, took over the brigade from then-acting Commander Tacic on the 19th of May, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: 18th of May. On the 19th of May, the units were already in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So that's the point at which Tacic left and you took over?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, he asked you to stay and organise people in the area and to form brigades from the existing territorial units staffs; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is "he"? Is it Tacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- Tacic. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He asked me to form a brigade, not brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you. So with that clarification, Tacic asked you to form a brigade from the existing territorial unit staffs. And that's correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And in that context, the Birac Brigade was supposed to take over all the competencies of the TO Staffs; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the 6th of June when the TO Staffs ceased to exist and the commands of units of army -- of the Army of Republika Srpska came into being. From the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we'll look at the 6th June order in a moment. But prior to that time, you had been instructed by Tacic -- or asked by Tacic, consistent with the 12 May decision on forming the army, to form your brigade from the existing TOs. And in that context, you gave orders to the -- the existing TO Staffs to undertake certain actions, including providing you with units; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: No. The following is correct, if you permit me. Colonel Tacic handed over a file, complete documentation of the brigade, and all he said was, "May God help you. I'm going." And that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Understood. And I believe you've stated that previously. My question was a bit different. I understand that Tacic left and left you with responsibility to address the situation. But you referred to the -- to 6 June, on which date there was an order that we'll see in a moment. That was the order to absorb or incorporate the existing TO Staffs and the units in their entirety; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Renamed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Gradually to rename them to the commands of the Army of Republika Srpska, and in some municipalities this lasted for weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But prior to that time, consistent with the 12 May decision that we referred to earlier and consistent with what Tacic told you about assuming all the competencies, you gave orders to those TO Staffs to yield units, to form units to undertake or not undertake actions and so on; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: I did not issue such an order. I acted pursuant to an order of the 15th of May, 1992, from Colonel Tacic. Pursuant to an order. You have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wasn't suggesting that you initiated the process, General, just that you followed up on that by issuing necessary orders to the TO Staffs as required; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Individually, yes, correct. Because all actions were carried out pursuant to the order by Tacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we will, in a moment after the adjournment, get to the issue of whether or not you have consistently maintained that all actions were carried out pursuant to the order by Tacic. But before then, let me continue with some of the chronology that leads to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I see the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps it won't be before that. When we resume after the break, I will just address one more item before we discuss some of those orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, Mr. Andric. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can meanwhile call up 65 ter 31629 and go to -- well, we'll leave it at the cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, just before we adjourned I indicated that I had one additional document I wanted to bring to your attention by way of backdrop before discussing some of the documents and orders mentioned in your statement. On the screen now before you, you see a document dated 20 May 1992 from General Dencic, as you will see on the last page of the document in the moment. And it's a document describing the current political and military situation. First of all, Dencic was the commander of the 17th Corps of the JNA which formed the basis of the East Bosnia Corps, correct, and he became - at least for a time - the commander of the East Bosnia Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2 in the English and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There we see toward the top of the page in English and in the second paragraph in B/C/S, General Dencic indicates, in this case four days after the strategic objectives were announced at the 16th Assembly Session in Banja Luka, that the situation is that the Serbian people "must struggle for complete separation from the Muslim and Croatian peoples and form its own state."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we scroll up in the English version, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, you were made aware either directly through this document or from general information provided by the command of the East Bosnia Corps of this position of the political and military leadership regarding the need for complete separation from the Muslim and Croatian peoples; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: I couldn't have known on the 20th in view of the fact that on the 19th I had just arrived in the area of responsibility of the future brigade. On the 20th, I was asking myself, "Here did I come?" I needed to get acquainted with the situation and find my feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. Eventually, however, this information, that is, the information we've just focused on regarding the need for complete separation, was conveyed to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So it's your position before this Court that you were never aware during the entire pendency of your service in the VRS of the objective of separation from the Muslim and Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, you're putting a different question now. First you asked specifically about the date. And it's normal when Bosnia was illegally recognised as a sovereign country that the government, or rather the Serbian state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, reached the decision on the 7th --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I'm sorry to interrupt you. Sorry to interrupt you. I'm not asking you for your dissertation on the logic of the situation. I focused you on what General Dencic stated in his military and political situation assessment. You indicated that you were not aware of that on the 20th, the date this was issued, and then I asked you if you became aware of that. And you indicated no. So that's all I'm clarifying. Did you become aware of the fact that one of the political and military objectives was complete separation from the Muslim and Croats?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: After the referendum on the 1st of March, 1992, when the Muslims voted to remain in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serbs then said no, we will remain in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I take it that's by way of your explanation for how you consider that this military and political situation assessment came about. That wasn't my question but we'll move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would tender 65 ter 31629.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document receives number P7345.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we now call up P466.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, this is a document dated 28 May 1992 which bears your name and signature. First of all, this is your order; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that is your signature; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is an order of the 28th of May, 1992, to the Zvornik Territorial Defence Staff. And as we can see, it begins by noting that nothing had been done until that date to set up the 6th Infantry Brigade, the AA Defence Light Artillery Division or the tank company, preventing you from placing those units under your command. And then after that preface, you go on, pursuant to the order on the organisation of defence dated 15 May 1992 by Colonel Tacic, order a number of things including the -- ordering the Zvornik TO Staff to carry out the formation of those previously mentioned units; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: May I just correct you? The heading does not deal with the formation of the 6th Infantry Brigade but the 6th Infantry Battalion. This is a major difference. The rest is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But be that as it may, the document says "brigade." Are you saying the document is incorrect; therefore, you're correcting it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least in the English it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: PB stands for what? Could you tell us that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's an infantry battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the translation may have to be revised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll be happy to submit it for that purpose, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if it's possible at all because B, battalion, brigade, both words start, at least in English, with a B, and from what I understand also in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but I think for "brigade" there is a different acronym, like Br.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A brigade cannot form brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That will be revised. Let's move on meanwhile in the understanding of the answer the witness has given as to the battalion rather than brigade. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then in item 6 of the order, you direct that: "The moving out of the Muslim population must be organised and co-ordinated with the municipalities through which the moving is carried out. Only women and children can move out, while men fit for military service are to be placed in camps for exchange." Now, in paragraph 4 of your statement, General, you state that the -- and that is your statement that was admitted here in Court today. You state that the order to move out Muslim residents "referred to only those Muslims who expressed the wish to go." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this last item, the Birac Serbian Autonomous Region, or District, government adopted the same order; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we can call up quickly P190.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's an order of the 31st of May, 1992, by you. And as we see in the preface, it references that decision by the Birac Serbian Autonomous Region government; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And the decision by the Birac government, SAO government, was adopted for the same reasons as your order; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: The decision by the SAO Birac government is something that I don't know what it was based on. You have to ask them. But I can say that it was adopted. But in my opinion, which may or may not be true, but on the 22nd of May, 1992, an agreement was signed between all the parties and Madam Ogata on the way in which the population will move out, and I think that the leadership was guided by that agreement, by those signatures on the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, General, I was referring specifically to paragraph 4 of the statement that was admitted in evidence here in Court today where you state -- and you discuss item 6 of this order and state that: "It is for these very reasons that the local civil authorities also adopted the decision to organise the moving out of the Muslims." So you state that --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: I accept that. I do, I accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I directed your attention to that, in particular, General, because, in fact, the official reason given at the time, that is given contemporaneously for this order to move out the Muslims, was not that it was a response to requests by Muslims to be permitted to leave but that it was adopted as a result of crimes Muslim extremists carried out against Serbs in the area. That was the reason given at the time for the order to move out the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: That was in one paragraph of the Serbian government decision. I -- I read it. It's one of the reasons. But as far as Muslims, Croats, and Serbs are concerned, that was the date they agreed to move out the population. The government of Birac called upon the population of Tuzla, Kladanj, and other places to organise the safe moving out of the population, taking particular care about the protection of each of the three ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The intention to address the perceived problem of crimes carried out against Serbs by armed Muslims would not be addressed, General, would it, by the -- by a course of action to simply allow those Muslims who wished to leave to depart in an organised way, would it? In short, if you are concerned about the people who are attacking you and want to fight, letting a certain number of other people go is not going to address that problem.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me. I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, the question is this: The Birac -- this decision to move out the Muslims was officially described as the result of - and, therefore, the intention to address - crimes allegedly committed against Serbs in the area, and that meant moving out Muslims whether they wanted to or not; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: That's one segment. One segment. And there are many segments. In the area of responsibility of the Birac Brigade and in the municipality, there were many armed individuals, units of the TO, units of the Crisis Staffs of local communes on the Muslim side. Then there were many paramilitary formations that were dangerous, dangerous from a security point of view not only for Muslims but also for Serbs, and I think that the leadership was guided by other segments, including this one; that is to say, stop and prevent liquidations on both sides because we had armed people then at that time. Also, soldiers in civilian clothes, screening, triage had to take place in order to see who did what. All of these are segments that the government of SAO Birac was guided by, and of course my order was written in that context as well. Not at a single moment was it written in order to have somebody killed. On the contrary. The only aim was to protect people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, this Court has received evidence that on June 6th, in the official publication Javnost, the decision to move out the Muslims was announced, the reason given as stated in Javnost is: "The government decided to take this step as a result of crimes Muslim extremists carried out against Serbs in the area." And no other reason is given. That's P3737. Were you aware at the time, General, that the only official reason given for the decision to move out the Muslims was that it was taken because of crimes allegedly carried out against Serbs in the area by Muslim extremists?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask - perhaps if would be fairer towards the witness - to be given P3737 so that he could see what it is that the Prosecutor is asking him about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No problem. I thought the question was brief enough that it didn't require that. But if we could call up P3737, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You'll see that on the top left, General, and you will be able to quickly see the reference that I made: The government decided to take this step as a result of crimes Muslim extremists carried out against Serbs in the area.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, if we want to go back, I can. I thought that was a waste of time. I Just referred to one segment. This is what date, the 30th of May, is it? Is that right, the 30th of May? We'll be being back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The article refers to the decision of the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, let me just tell you the Tuzla column occurred on the 15th of May. You know yourself how many people were killed then. Let's not waste time now. Then the municipality of Kalesija, where I was born by the way. All the Serb villages. All the people there were killed. Also on the 7th of April, the Muslim side organised units and they stopped a column of the regular army. Please. You asked me about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I'm sorry -- no, I didn't ask you that question, sir. Let me -- can I assume based on your answer -- General, can I assume based on what you're just saying that you're explaining to me why this decision was adopted for those reasons, for the reason given in the article; correct? You explained to me the backdrop -- what you say is the backdrop to the decision to move out the Muslims as a result of crimes committed against Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: I can just speak of one segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we have the -- that's the information, okay. And you're indicating to me you're speaking about that particular segment of what you understand to be the order. I think you've made that clear before.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the speaker. There are too many microphones on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, the interpreters could not hear your last remark. If you could repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: What I said is that that is only part of that segment. But you did not allow me to speak about the other crimes that were committed before this decision was reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Understood. Well, let's set aside for the moment the contemporaneous explanation for the decision to move out the Muslims. In any event, General, many of the people who were moved out were rounded up or captured before they expressed any desire to leave. And specifically at the moment, I'm referring to what you have previously said about the portion of your order directed at the men fit for military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So let's turn back to P466.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As we see in item 6, it provides that men fit for military service are to be placed in camps for exchange. And as you've explained in paragraph 5 of your statement, that portion of the order refers to "after they were captured, we first had to establish who among them had been active participants in armed conflict." So this -- the -- this portion of the order, referring to men fit for military service, refers to a body of people who were captured. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: What is written there is able-bodied military-aged men should be separated. They should be identified. One should see who it was that had taken part in the armed conflict -- armed conflicts. Whether anyone of them had committed any crimes against the civilian population or whether they had assisted the armed forces of the enemy in some other way. All of that, because we, in the Tuzla canton - Zivinice, Kladanj, Olovo - had a large number of POWs. From my village, Jeginov Lug specifically, all old men were taken to the public security station in Tuzla, all of them over the age of 60. So thanks to that and other people that we had in the camps we exchanged these people. So the aim was not to have liquidations take place because in Zvornik we had many paramilitary units, many paramilitary units. After all, I think that we are wasting time as far as this order is concerned. On the 31st, I issued an order by way of a request, a plea to the TO staff where I ask the commander of the TO Staff, since he had not organised units, that he send me an officer for further co-ordinated action. So it is pointless to talk about all of this because my order was never accepted by the commander of the TO Staff. So we're wasting time because this was never materialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you have just stated, and you stated before, that between the time of your May 28th order to the Zvornik TO command and the time of the May 31st handwritten document to which you've just referred where you make a request rather than an order, you came to realise that your order of May 28th had not been obeyed because the Zvornik TO Staff made decisions independently. That's what you state in your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me call up first 65 ter 32496.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that. Witness, could you please explain to me -- you said these people even over 60, we had them there and they were exchanged. That was good for them, that's how I understood your testimony, because they would be safe. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That pertained to Serb civilians from the municipality of Kalesija, Jeginov Lug who had been arrested and taken to prison in Tuzla. They were over the age of 60, most of them; elderly men, women, and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you then said: "So thanks to that and other people that we had in the camps we exchanged these people. So the aim was not to have liquidations take place because in Zvornik we had many paramilitary units ..." I understood that there was some fear that the paramilitary units in Zvornik might harm the people which you had then in the camps. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, this includes non-military -- non-soldiers, even if they would have been at -- of military age. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It says there unambiguously, military age, able-bodied men. That's what it says in my statement and in the explanation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But still if you're able bodied and of military age, that doesn't make you a soldier, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely right. But next it says to carry out screening, triage. So if somebody had not committed a crime, had not taken part in armed conflicts, then these people would be released, and they could go to Muslim territory if that is what they wished to do. Now those who expressed the wish to say, could stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So they were not put there for exchange but -- I'm again -- but looking at the document, I don't think it says that they were there to be investigated, whether they had committed crimes or not. You added that. But that's not found in the document, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this other document of the 30th, I order that the security organ interview people and supply all the necessary information to the command. So to check, to double-check who out of these people took part in war crimes or committed some other crime. And then from these camps, Your Honour, those who had not done anything were released from these camps and went towards Kladanj. I will give you many examples, many dates when we organised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So they were not exchanged but you just released them to be free to do what they wanted to do. Is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Those who wished to remain in Republika Srpska could stay, and those who wished to leave could go towards Kalesija, Zivinice, Tuzla, or Cerska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you keep records of those who were not exchanged but were offered freedom to go wherever they wanted to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you will see later that I as brigade commander ordered the battalion commander in Vlasenica to work out an entire paper about security, accommodation, everything that has to do with POWs and everything the POWs are entitled to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's prisoners of war. But I'm talking about that category of persons who were not soldiers, though perhaps of military age and able-bodied, who were free to go. That's not POWs. That's a different category. And I asked you, and have not answered that question, whether you -- whether you kept a record of those who were free to go, was -- did you keep such a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't have information now about documentation of that kind. This selection was made automatically. They left. I really cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, automatically. They were put in those camps on your order. Doesn't that bring a certain responsibility to verify whether what was not found in the order; but, as you explained it to us now, that they were sent there for triage and that everyone was automatically free to go, wouldn't it be your responsibility after you had ordered them to be detained also to look after, that they were not treated as prisoners of war but that they were treated as civilians free to go wherever they wanted to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I repeat, at brigade level, every brigade has a location where POWs are assembled. At such a location, a triage takes place. So prepare not taken to a camp, but it on this location that the triage takes place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, indeed, you are repeating your answer and it's still not an answer to my question. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, what's on the screen now is an order dated the 30th of May, 1992, by East Bosnia Corps Commander Dencic, providing that the Zvornik municipal TO is to be transformed into the command of the Zvornik infantry brigade of the East Bosnian Corps of the Army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. General, what happened between May 28th, 1992, when you gave the Zvornik TO an order to do what they hadn't done previously, and May 31st, your handwritten note to them where you make a request for co-ordination, is that you learned that the Zvornik TO was not independent but was simply going to become a sister brigade in the East Bosnia Corps. That's the reality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: If I understood your question, the document of the 31st of May itself shows that I am requesting, kindly asking the TO Staff to send an officer to me in order to organise co-ordinated action. From that, one can see that I did not have any power over the TO Staff at all because basically they were not carrying out my order of the 28th May. They were not establishing units as I had said, and they were using them without my approval. At will. So I was not in command at a single point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, my question was different. You relied upon the May 31st request to the Zvornik TO command in contrast to your May 28th order to indicate to this Court that that demonstrated that the Zvornik TO was independent. The reality was that up to the 28th, you were aware of the chain of command and knew that you had the power to order the Zvornik TO to do things; but by the 31st you had learned that they were going to be transformed into a sister brigade, not that you found out they were some kind of independent group. That's the reality.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn then to 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could tender 32496 before we move onto another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document receives number P7346.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7346 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to 65 ter 32499, English page 71, B/C/S page 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is your testimony before the Belgrade Court conducting the trial of Branko Grujic and Marko Pavlovic. And there you state: As early as on the 31st I received information, since the municipality president had asked that the Zvornik Brigade be established, there was no longer any point for me to insist on the establishment because it was only a matter of three days. And then as early on the 31st, was forced to propose that we co-operate. And similarly if we turn to page 64 in the English and page 35 in the Serbian, you state in the course of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have to wait for the B/C/S to appear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You state in the course of discussing what happened in the three days between the May 28th order and the 31st May request, that you: "... received information that the Zvornik Brigade was being established. Then there was no point for two or three days to cause problems regarding organisations and reorganisation." So, General, contrary to what you just told the Court, that you didn't know that the Zvornik TO was about to be transformed into a sister brigade, that's precisely what you knew and precisely what you told the Belgrade Court in 2007; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: I said that to the court and I'm not denying that. However, it's politicians, local politicians that were planning that. As for the chain of command, I did not receive any orders. So for me, the superior command is the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll be tendering those excerpts, Mr. President, but I believe there may well be more so we may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could have a number reserved for it. Madam Registrar could you reserve a number for the excerpts of these court proceedings in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number would be P7347.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That number is reserved. Mr. Tieger, if you have done with this page. Witness, I read a little bit further down in that page: "Because I know that Mr. Grujic kept insisting on the establishment of the Zvornik Brigade, because they have their own brigade, and I absolutely supported this and requested the superior command to have the Zvornik Brigade established as soon as possible." Now, that's not the TO acting independently but that is the Zvornik TO becoming the Zvornik Brigade with a common superior command, your brigade, and the Zvornik Brigade. Therefore, I do not fully understand what you mean if you say they acted independently. Perhaps independently from you, but they acted under the same superior command which you addressed to encourage the quick establishment of the Zvornik Brigade. That's how I understand what you're saying here and what I have difficulties in reconciling with the TO acting independently. Any comment on what I just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you understood this well. The TO acted independently in relation to the army because it was only on the 6th of June that an order was made for the units and the staffs of the TO to be renamed into commands of units of the Army of Republika Srpska. That process in certain municipalities lasted up until the end of the year, even. I can guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, the fact is that the Zvornik Brigade, by way of example, was established in actual fact on the 2nd of June and, indeed, Colonel Blagojevic received the brigade on the 2nd of June; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now you refer to the 6th of June. But as we discussed before, that was the Ilic order, which this Court has received, that's P3739, of the 6th of June, absorbing or incorporating all the current TO Staffs, not just portions of their units, into the Army of Republika Srpska. And, in fact, you implemented that order on the 8th of June; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you that is an order of the 8th of June. In order to rename all these staffs and units, that requires time. Commander Blagojevic, the brigade commander, when he arrived, he established the brigade. And the TO Staff functioned along parallel lines in terms of Colonel Blagojevic. I've been trying to explain that all the time, but it seems that I haven't succeeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Firstly quickly, 65 ter 32497.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is your order implementing the order of the East Bosnia Corps command on the 6th of June, to which we referred a moment ago, and which is also pursuant to Article 2 of the decision to establish the Army of the Serbian Republic of BH, which you referred to earlier on in your testimony, and it provides that those TO Staffs and units shall all be renamed commands and units of the Army of the Serbian Republic and that all of them, the units and the staffs, shall become part -- that is, all of them in the above-mentioned municipalities shall become part of the Birac Brigade. That's correct, isn't it? That's your order making those provisions and directing those actions to be taken?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my order, correct. But I have already explained to you the process of establishment and how TO Staffs and units grew into units of the Army of Republika Srpska. To understand what I've been saying more easily, the Supreme Command, and everyone knows who the Supreme Commander is, Mr. Karadzic, is responsible for establishing units and organising them. And it's only on the 21st of May that an organisational order was issued, and general mobilisation was -- actually in order to mobilise the army, the armed people, the military-aged population, you need at least a month in order to carry out mobilisation. So up until the end of the war, we had some of these staffs that we could not -- could not fit into the units of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, the reality is that both before and after its incorporation or transformation into the Zvornik Brigade, that is, the transformation which took place on the 2nd of June, the Zvornik TO was implementing the moving out of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: I cannot discuss that because I really wasn't involved in that. So you cannot really ask me about things that I'm not informed about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, General, I'm going to suggest that giving an order to the Zvornik TO on the 28th of May regarding the moving out of the Muslims and the placing of military-age men in camps for exchange does involve you. And in that respect, I want to take a look at some of the evidence of what was happening in Zvornik at that time. So, first -- well, given the time perhaps it's best to break and pick it up when we resume. If we have -- I don't know -- if we have two minutes, I'm wrong. Then if we have -- okay. Then it's probably best to break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll take a break. Witness, would you please follow the usher. We'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I failed to tender 32497, the 8 June 1992 order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number would be P7348.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. We take a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, Mr. Tieger will now continue his cross-examination. Is there a matter you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I wanted to suggest the following in order to use our time better, not to deal with Zvornik because I have no responsibilities or authority there. I think we have more burning problems and it seems to me that the time is going very slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the parties decide on what matter they want to examine you. If you are concerned about not wasting time, I would suggest that you carefully listen to the question and answer that question alone. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, before we adjourned I indicated to you that I was going to direct your attention to evidence of what happened in Zvornik between the time of your May 28th order, including item 6 regarding the moving out of the Muslims, and the time that the Zvornik TO became the Zvornik Brigade on the 2nd of June. And in that respect, I wanted to direct your attention to P425, evidence in the Karadzic case. That's at e-court page 4. As I advised my friends from the Defence, I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
